analysis.one_liner: Bars dumping mining and other waste into rivers and streams as "fill" material.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 76 House cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote; it died in committee when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Clean Water Act's definition of "fill material" so that waste dumped into a river, lake, or stream no longer counts as legal "fill." Its main target is the practice of mountaintop removal coal mining, where companies blast off mountaintops and push the leftover rock and dirt — and the buried streams underneath — into adjacent valleys. By classifying that waste as waste rather than fill, the bill would make those valley fills subject to pollution permits and, in practice, nearly impossible to continue.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream from streams receiving dumped waste — especially Appalachian communities below mountaintop removal coal mines — would gain cleaner water, unburied streams, and less flooding and sediment. Anyone who fishes, swims, or draws drinking water downstream of a waste-dumping site also gains.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Appalachian communities near mountaintop removal mines

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Clean Water Act to define "fill material" as any pollutant that replaces waters of the United States with dry land or changes a water body's bottom elevation, but expressly excludes any pollutant discharged "primarily to dispose of waste," so waste can no longer be permitted as fill [S2] [S3].

Under that definition, the rock, dirt, and debris pushed into valleys by mountaintop removal mining would be treated as discharged waste rather than legal fill, bringing those dumps under the Clean Water Act's pollution permitting rules [S2] [S3].

The practical effect would be to stop or sharply reduce the burial of headwater streams under mine waste, protecting the water sources and stream systems that downstream communities rely on [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies that practice mountaintop removal mining would bear the main cost: they could no longer cheaply dispose of mine waste by pushing it into valleys and streams, and would have to contain it on land — a real expense. Some construction and dredging projects that involve placing waste materials in water would also face tighter permitting.

drawbacks.text: The industry's core objection was that reclassifying mine waste as waste would make disposal far more expensive and threaten mining jobs in coal-dependent Appalachian communities, since valleys and streams are currently the cheapest disposal route [S2] [S3].

The new definition applies to "any pollutant" discharged to dispose of waste, not just mine waste, so a broad range of projects placing waste-derived material in water could face new permitting costs or litigation over what counts as "primarily" waste disposal [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge that ending valley fills does not erase the demand for coal; it shifts disposal costs, and coal-dependent local economies would absorb some of the pain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people living in and below the affected watersheds, the benefit is direct and large: intact streams and cleaner water instead of valleys buried under mine waste. The cost falls on a specific, highly profitable industry and on the small share of local jobs tied to mountaintop removal operations. The main design weakness is breadth — the exclusion for waste applies to all dischargers, not just miners, which could create compliance questions beyond the bill's target. On balance, the bill's burden falls on a concentrated industry whose disposal method imposes its costs on the public's water.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced and sent to its Water Resources subcommittee the next day, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ) introduced the Clean Water Protection Act on May 26, 2005, with 52 original cosponsors signing on the first day [S1] [S3].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and on May 27 it was referred to the subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment [S5].

Support grew to 76 cosponsors — 68 Democrats, 7 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but the bill never advanced out of committee, and its last action in the record is that subcommittee referral [S4] [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007, having never received a hearing, markup, or vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies practicing mountaintop removal came out ahead: without a change in law, they could keep classifying mine waste as "fill" and dumping it into valleys and streams. The committee leadership that never acted on a bill backed by 76 members also preserved the permitting status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal companies dumping mine waste in valleys

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 52 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 76 House cosponsors (68 Democrats, 7 Republicans, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including a bipartisan group of Republicans, signaling broad House support.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — in a committee that reports most water legislation.

against.name: Coal mining industry (mountaintop removal operators)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a threat to the mountaintop removal disposal method, which depends on dumping mine waste into valleys as "fill."

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 68 of 76 — but included 7 Republicans and 1 Independent, so the bill had genuine bipartisan backing that never translated into committee action.

industries.note: The bill's central target: mine operators blast mountaintops and push the waste into valleys, burying streams, under rules that let waste count as "fill." The bill would reclassify that waste as waste, ending the cheapest disposal route. The industry's savings come directly at the expense of downstream communities' water.

industries.industry: Dredging, construction, and land development firms placing fill in water
industries.note: Projects that dispose of waste material into water would face the same exclusion and stricter permitting, raising costs. Legitimate structural fill — dirt, rock, sand used to build — would remain permitted under the bill's definition.
